newsitem.title: USA: Fedders Q2 seen hurt by higher inventories.
newsitem.headline: Fedders Q2 seen hurt by higher inventories.

text.p: Fedders Corp reported a first quarter loss and said higher air conditioner inventories will hurt results, particularly in the first fiscal half, ending February 28.
Fedders said first quarter sales increased 19.0 percent to $33.1 million as international shipments and non-air conditioning shipments more than offset a decline in domestic air conditioner sales.
The net loss for the normally unprofitable off-season quarter was $1.2 million, or $0.05 per share.

The company said the loss compared with an unusual quarterly profit of $0.01 per share in the prior year that reflected strong domestic shipments of room air conditioners following three hot summers in a row.

The unusually cold summer of 1996, in the Northeast and Upper Midwest, has led to greatly increased end-of-season inventories at both retailers and manufacturers, Fedders pointed out. Many manufacturers and importers who do not or cannot practice just-in-time delivery and accurate-response manufacturing had to take back end-of-season inventory from their retail customers.

These higher inventories at retailers and at other manufacturers will significantly impact 1997 demand and will affect its results, particularly in the first fiscal half -- already an off season for air conditioners and dehumidifiers.

"There are international challenges we will face in 1997 as well, Fedders said. "The weakening of the Japanese yen creates more global competition in air conditioning and compressors, and also in thermoelectric products such as those produced by Melcor, our other newly acquired business.

"And, the expanded infrastructure that we must build to support our growing international business will increase expenses in 1997, even while sales and profits are lower in North America," Fedders said.

From 1995 to 1996, Fedders said, it increased international sales to $24.5 million from $12.9 million; "and in 1997, we expect to better that performance with international sales in excess of $40 million.
"Climbing international sales serve as a hedge against cold summers in North America, such as the one just past, and in 1997, will partially offset lower North American sales."
